item.title: Brussels or Beijing? The EU’s ‘Made in Europe’ plans will force the UK to choose
item.description:
Brussels or Beijing? The EU’s ‘Made in Europe’ plans will force the UK to choose  Expert comment jon.wallace 29 October 2026

Either way, the UK will be forced to pay a price.

The EU’s Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) is pushing the UK toward an economic confrontation with China it would rather avoid. The IAA plans to introduce new ‘Made in Europe’ obligations, conditioning access to certain public subsidy and procurement schemes on the use of sufficient local, European, content. This is intended, in part, to protect European industry from cheap, high-quality, Chinese goods such as hybrid and electric vehicles (EVs). 

The UK government, seeking closer economic integration with the EU, wants ‘Made in Europe’ provisions extended to include its firms. But key EU member states are conditioning any extension on the UK aligning with EU economic security measures. 

A 15 October Franco-German paper said that ‘Made in Europe’ treatment for the automotive sector should only be extended to the UK and a small group of other partners on the condition of both reciprocity and ‘dynamic alignment with EU conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defense measures’. 

In practical terms, France and Germany want the UK to impose tariffs on Chinese EVs to prevent the further erosion of their manufacturers’ UK market share. They also want the UK to impose stricter conditions on foreign direct investment into key manufacturing sectors to prevent Chinese firms from qualifying for future EU subsidies or procurement schemes via their UK-located operations. 

With the next EU–UK summit scheduled for 20 November, this creates a problem for Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s new government. Much of the media reporting has focused on the question of whether the UK will agree to impose tariffs on Chinese vehicles. But the focus on investment is arguably more consequential, given the UK’s desire to attract Chinese automotive manufacturing facilities to Britain. 

The UK’s China problem

Until now, the UK’s preferred approach to China has been one of cautious pragmatism. It has demonstrated a willingness to intervene with tariffs or other restrictions in the event of acute economic or national security concerns. See, for example, the decision to impose permanently high tariffs on certain steel products or the blocking of a proposed £1.5 billion investment in offshore wind by the Chinese firm Ming Yang. 

Want to hear more on the future of global trade?

Join us at our Global Trade Conference for expert analysis on the shifting rules of the global economy.

However, the UK has continued to court Chinese investment in the automotive sector and deepen trade ties in what it considers non-sensitive areas. And, though it has made a commitment to the US to strengthen supply chain security in respect of steel and pharmaceuticals as part of the 2025 Economic Prosperity Deal, there has so far been limited evidence of substantive implementation. 

The UK’s reluctance to fully align with either the EU or US approach to China is understandable, given its relative size and economic weight. It wants increased trade and investment and relies on Chinese renewables for its decarbonization objectives. 

But the UK can certainly not afford to be shut out of EU procurement and public subsidy schemes. The EU’s proposed safeguard on hybrid vehicle imports – which would restrict imports above specified quota levels – will also create its own pressures, as Chinese vehicles risk being diverted onto the UK market. 

It is therefore less of a question of whether the UK will align itself with EU economic security measures than how.

The price to pay

One route would be for the UK to replicate EU measures wholesale. This would see the UK replicate EU tariffs on EVs and the new hybrid safeguard. And it could potentially include future interventions targeting chemicals, plastics, batteries and wind turbines. 

The UK would also need to consider equivalent restrictions on foreign investment, reflecting proposed IAA conditions relating to ownership limits, joint ventures, workforce localization and local content in key manufacturing sectors. 

Yet this approach is not straightforward. The UK does not necessarily have the legal tools available to replicate EU measures and has historically been cautious about breaching its international obligations. 

China would also be incentivized to retaliate. That could mean anything from initiating its own tariff measures against UK exports to imposing restrictions on rare earths or battery inputs.

The UK is not the only country in the region facing pressure from the EU to impose more stringent controls on Chinese trade and investment as a condition for access to the EU market. Turkey, Morocco and Switzerland are in a similar position. China will be wary of a negative precedent being established and keen to demonstrate that aligning with EU restrictions comes at a price. Indeed, Beijing may have a greater incentive to make an example of the UK than escalate its confrontation with the EU.

An alternative would be for the UK to pursue similar outcomes more slowly, using traditional trade defence tools. An anti-subsidy investigation into Chinese electric vehicles, for example, would take around a year to conclude but could provide the government with some breathing space. A safeguard investigation, potentially justified by rising Chinese imports and the risk of trade diversion from the EU, could offer a quicker route. 

Neither would guarantee the outcome the EU wants. And both would need to satisfy the relevant legal requirements. But they would at least allow the UK to argue that it was responding to evidence of harm to its own industry, rather than simply implementing EU demands. 

A safeguard also has the benefit, or not, of generally applying to imports regardless of origin, allowing the UK to argue it is not singling out China. It also remains possible that Brussels will attach more importance to the political signal of alignment than to the precise form of the measures adopted.

Yet this still leaves open the question of Chinese investment into UK manufacturing. This is of particular importance in the automotive sector. And it will prove more difficult to address without compromising the government’s wider economic objectives.

The government could also seek to demonstrate progress by announcing new economic security tools, such as a proposed anti-coercion instrument. It could also introduce specific restrictions on foreign investment, or repackage existing initiatives, such as new cybersecurity-related restrictions. Such announcements might demonstrate goodwill towards Brussels but they would not automatically satisfy EU demands for alignment on specific measures. 

The most likely outcome is that the UK seeks to navigate a course through these competing demands, giving the EU just enough of what it wants, while delaying implementation, hoping to avoid the worst response from Beijing. Delay may buy time with Brussels. But Beijing will likely view any such commitment as setting a precedent and retaliate against the UK accordingly. 

There will be a price for the UK to pay either way. The only question is how successfully the government can minimize it.

Trump wants Myanmar's rare earths. He's talking to the wrong people.
item.description:
The Trump administration is carrying out a major shift in U.S. policy toward Myanmar.

After the 2021 coup, the administration of former President Joe Biden demanded a return to democracy and sanctioned the military junta. Now, however, Washington is reportedly holding direct talks with the very people it accused of genocide in 2022.

Trump had already given Gen. Min Aung Hlaing implicit recognition when he sent him a tariff letter in July 2025. Two weeks later, the U.S. Treasury removed several of his cronies from its sanctions list. In June this year, officials from both countries met in Tokyo. But the most significant step came in mid-September, when Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance opened direct talks with Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyidaw, Myanmar’s capital, marking the highest-level U.S. contact since the coup.

The stated goals of U.S. reengagement are narrow: securing the release of U.S. businessman Adam Castillo, a former head of the American Chamber of Commerce in Myanmar, and enlisting the regime’s cooperation in shutting down the online scam centers operating in the country. U.S. officials also had their eyes on Myanmar's rare earth deposits, a market currently controlled by China.

The first goal has been achieved. On the second, the regime is part of the problem, and the third lies in territory it does not control. So is Trump betting on a partner that cannot deliver?

A bogged-down war


The current phase of the war began in mid-2021 when the crackdown on anti-coup protests pushed thousands of activists into the countryside where minority insurgencies had been operating for decades. Alongside the armed resistance, ousted lawmakers from the National League for Democracy, the ruling party prior to the coup, creating the National Unity Government (NUG). While some militant groups joined the NUG, others remained independent. The result is a conflict fragmented both politically and geographically, whose actors pursue different goals, shift alliances and tactics, and are tied to different foreign powers.

Over the following four years, the military lost control of much of the country to the NUG and ethnic armed organizations while keeping its grip on the main levers of the economy, such as ports, factories and offshore gas. But it lost access to most rare earth deposits, which are now held by minority groups like the Wa, Karens and Shan.

The Biden administration responded with targeted sanctions on the junta’s leaders and its business conglomerates, and supported pro-democracy groups through humanitarian and non-lethal aid, much of it channeled across the Thai border. There were never any weapons transfers or formal recognition of the NUG as a legitimate interlocutor.

Aid from the United States and Europe, said Khun Alynn, Deputy Head of Department of Home Affairs, Interim Executive Council of Karenni State (IEC), “came through humanitarian organizations, but also through third countries that I can’t confirm.”

Then, in 2025, the incoming Trump administration dismantled USAID, just as the military launched a counteroffensive and began retaking territory with new tactics and drones supplied by Russia and China.

“The [USAID] cuts had a huge impact. Medical supplies are already running short, and we can’t deal with the malaria and tuberculosis outbreaks in the area. At least two hospitals are going to close by the end of the year,” Paung, a 35-year-old doctor and director of the Luke Foundation, told Responsible Statecraft.

Five years of war have taken a staggering toll: according to the UN, more than 3.7 million people are internally displaced, and violence monitor ACLED has recorded 100,114 conflict-related deaths. In Karenni, Maw Re Ree, deputy head of the IEC's humanitarian department, works in the region's roughly 500 displacement camps. "We systematically receive threats of bombing," she said.

Sovereignty problems


The junta retains formal sovereignty but controls only about 21% of Myanmar’s territory; resistance forces hold some 42%, and the rest is contested. To consolidate his position, in January 2026, Min Aung Hlaing held an election in only those parts of the country that were under his control and was sworn in as president of a nominally civilian government in a ceremony attended by representatives of China, India and Thailand, along with 20 other countries, last April. Western governments dismissed the vote as a sham, while Washington stayed silent.

That silence has left the opposition uneasy, especially in light of the administration’s recent moves. “The military regime may also seek to use engagement with the United States to overcome its crisis of political legitimacy,” Zin Mar Aung, the NUG’s foreign minister, told Responsible Statecraft.

Washington’s priority appears to be curbing the financial losses and the harm to Americans caused by online scams and drug trafficking. The scam compounds, located near the Thai border, are run by criminal syndicates and protected by junta-allied militias, such as the Border Guard Forces, which receive financial kickbacks from the scammers. Given this relationship and the power of the criminal syndicates, the regime “cannot fully guarantee” an end to these practices, Zin Mar Aung noted.

Rare earths, meanwhile, are “entirely off-limits to Naypyidaw,” said David Gum Awng, the NUG’s deputy foreign minister, referring to Myanmar’s capital.

Indeed, in late 2024, the Kachin Independence Army (KIA) seized the heart of one of the world's most valuable concentrations of heavy rare earths, and it taxes the trade with China to fund its fight. Further east, in territory controlled by the United Wa State Army (UWSA), which has remained neutral in the ongoing civil war, Chinese companies are mining rare earths, also without Naypyidaw's approval.

The options floated in Washington have ranged from dealing with the military authorities to brokering talks between them and the KIA, to engaging the KIA directly and possibly partnering with India to process the minerals. Each of those paths runs through Naypyidaw or bypasses the opposition coalition, which narrows the resistance’s room for maneuver without forcing an open break.

“So we're taking it very cautiously, but we also understand the very pragmatic nature of the world order that we live in,”said David Gum Awng, who noted that the NUG still maintains some contact with Washington.

The cost of the bet


For Napas Thein, a research fellow at the University of Toronto’s Myanmar Policy and Community Knowledge Hub, engaging the junta would cost Washington “credibility regarding democracy and human rights” and draw it into a highly unstable landscape. It would also strain U.S. ties with the resistance groups that control much of the country, and bring it closer to a regime aligned with Iran and North Korea.

What can the United States gain from a government that is partly financed by a criminal economy and does not control rare earths mines, Washington’s chief interest? The answer remains unclear.

Meanwhile, the war continues to drag on, and civilians continue to suffer. Just recently, a regime airstrike killed 50 people, including women and children, in a town in rebel-held Rakhine state.

item.title: Suited and booted: How Joseph Kabila went from president to rebel leader
As Trump blows up the Mideast, regional leaders look to Europe
item.description:
“Anything’s possible” was Donald Trump’s response when asked if he would launch a new attack on Iran after the midterm elections. Fears of what a return to all-out war would bring have set off a flurry of diplomacy. Two noteworthy tracks from European and regional powers have emerged as last-gasp attempts to prevent, or at least limit, the destruction a renewed conflict would cause. If they succeed, they could become the pillars of a new “coalition of the willing” to stabilise the Middle East without America in the lead.

The negotiators


The first track brings together the E4—Britain, France, Germany and Italy—and the R4 of Egypt, Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia. The foreign ministers of the E4+R4 met in Istanbul on October 23rd to discuss preserving the viability of a two-state solution in Israel-Palestine, ending the US-Iran war, reopening the Strait of Hormuz and defending Saudi Arabia against the latest offensive launched by the Houthis, a Yemeni rebel group.

On the European side, the addition of Italy to the E3 is welcome. It bolsters Europe’s diplomatic weight, offsetting Britain’s Brexit-induced weakness and Germany’s loss of regional influence over its staunch support for Israel. Berlin’s relations with Tehran have also been tense since 2022, when Iran’s human-rights abuses and its military assistance to Russia soured ties. Italy does not carry the same baggage, nor did it take part in the E3’s decision last year to trigger the “snapback” of sanctions on Iran. That could eventually help it reopen the path to negotiations.

The Istanbul meeting also showed how far the R4 has come since it formed earlier this year in response to the shifting power balance in the Middle East. All its members but Egypt signed the Mecca Defence Alliance, a military pact, in August. The pact was recently tested when members activated the collective defence measures in response to the Houthi offensive against Saudi Arabia. The grouping signals that the region’s powers are increasingly willing to take responsibility for their own security.

The second diplomatic track opened three days after the Istanbul gathering, when security chiefs from Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia met Iran’s leaders in Tehran. The meeting was an attempt by regional powers to avert a new round of fighting by including Iran in a serious diplomatic process. It also allowed Iran to host, giving it a PR victory at a time when the Trump administration is attempting to impose a full blockade on the country.

These regional powers are scrambling to de-escalate as Tehran has made clear that its response to renewed US or Israeli strikes would be far more damaging than anything the Middle East has absorbed in the past eight months. It has already shown its reach through its ally in Yemen. In recent weeks the Houthis have damaged critical infrastructure inside Saudi Arabia and attacked shipping through the Red Sea. A joint effort by the Houthis and Iran to disrupt transit through two vital waterways—the straits of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb—would have global economic ramifications. Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia probably also warned Iran during the Tehran meeting that further strikes on its neighbours’ critical infrastructure and civilian targets would undo any prospect of regional integration.

A coalition of the middle


Whether these tracks succeed or fail, they point to a changing reality. Most glaring is America’s absence from both meetings, as European and regional powers increasingly try to work around an unpredictable Washington rather than with it. For the R4, the Trump administration’s handling of Iran has shattered the assumption that America’s armed forces offer iron-clad protection to its allies, a reality Europeans are also confronting over Ukraine. America and Israel might have the military capacity to devastate the region, but they have proved unable or unwilling to win the peace. Left to pick up the pieces, Middle Eastern and European countries have been made all too aware that stronger diplomatic efforts are needed for their own security.

If war and maximum pressure pushed Iran, a country of more than 90 million people, towards state collapse, the consequences for its neighbours and Europe would be disastrous. This is particularly so given that neither America nor Israel is likely to invest the time and money needed to rebuild it. Yet the Islamic Republic’s elite will probably remain in power for the foreseeable future. And as the Tehran meeting showed, the hard-line military factions that the war has brought to the fore currently dominate decision-making.

Averting disaster


The immediate priority for both tracks is to prevent a return to high-intensity war. It remains to be seen whether the E4+R4 can exert influence over both Trump and Tehran to end the conflict and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. But their combined leverage, if used with greater purpose and willingness, could add new force to diplomacy.

Teaming up more actively with the R4 would also give Europe better access to Washington and Tehran, both of which have increasingly dismissed European influence. That would improve Europe’s chances of advancing two of its strategic objectives: ensuring the peaceful nature of Iran’s future nuclear programme, and stabilising the Middle East. The E4 and R4 could also use their combined economic clout to press China to use its deep trade ties with Iran to secure the lasting reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.

The regional powers have also seen an advantage in fostering deeper cooperation with Europe. Relative to Russia, China and the US, Europeans can provide a more reliable partnership in security, defence and economic affairs. As the R4 countries seek to strengthen their defences, modernise their militaries and heal their economies after successive wars, Europe remains an attractive partner.

The E4 could also help middle powers in the region contain and potentially moderate the behaviour of both Israel and Iran. Europeans could restrain Israeli military activity in Lebanon and Syria through stronger economic and technical support to central governments and increased funding for the Lebanese Armed Forces. The R4 will similarly look to European countries to expand measures targeting Israeli occupation policies and illegal settlements.

On Iran, Europe and its regional partners could use the prospect of eventual sanctions relief to nudge Tehran towards a stronger agreement on its nuclear programme and reducing its destabilising conduct in the Middle East. The E4 and R4 share concerns that in a future deal with Iran, Washington may be willing to curtail the role of the International Atomic Energy Agency in monitoring Iran’s nuclear activities. Europeans could therefore make EU sanctions relief conditional on enhanced international monitoring, whatever Washington agrees bilaterally with Iran. The R4 could reinforce this by offering to be the first to invest in Iran’s post-sanctions economy, given that European companies, wary of reputational exposure, are likely to be slower to return.

Both the E4 and R4 view Iran’s missile and drone programme as a direct threat. Yet precisely because of its demonstrated effectiveness in the past year, Tehran is unlikely to negotiate a major rollback. Instead, the E4 and R4 could intensify efforts to slow Iran’s advances by disrupting supply chains from China and Russia and interdicting shipments to groups such as Hizbullah and the Houthis. They could also press Beijing to demand that Iran halt technology transfers to non-state armed actors.

Security without superpowers


The E4+R4 format creates opportunities for Europeans and regional powers to lay the foundations of a broader security architecture for the Middle East, one that goes beyond the deterrence framework envisaged by the Mecca pact. In the long run, it could even include Iran and Israel by merging the Tehran track and the Abraham Accords into a single process. Europe’s own experience with security mechanisms across the EU could prove useful in de-escalating tensions, managing military capabilities, and, eventually, building shared security and prosperity.

A return to full-scale war between America and Iran may be inevitable given Trump’s zero-sum instincts and apparent desire for a hard-power legacy. But even if the E4+R4 effort falters, it points to an emerging order shaped by the region’s middle powers. These countries are now looking to Europe, not America, to shore up their diplomacy. For Europeans, it is a chance to bring their diplomatic weight to bear after a long period of marginal influence in the Middle East. The initiative’s underlying commitment to de-escalation and a more inclusive diplomatic approach is precisely what the region needs.

This article was republished with permission from the European Council on Foreign Relations.

item.title: The Saudi-UAE split is ending. That may be bad news for Yemen.
item.description:
The Houthis’ lightning advances in Yemen have given Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates an opening to set aside their differences after a notable rupture over the country’s political makeup less than a year ago.

However, even if a unified threat manages to bind them together, their unresolved disagreements over the future of Yemen could limit the effectiveness of renewed military cooperation against the Houthis and deepen fragmentation elsewhere in Yemen.

At least for now, both countries have signaled a willingness to compartmentalize their disputes. Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman’s meeting with UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed on October 18 provided a public indication of renewed dialogue, with bin Salman praising the “historical relations between our two brotherly countries.”

The official readout did not announce a Yemen military agreement, but the Guardian separately reported that Abu Dhabi had agreed to resume payments to government-aligned forces it had previously backed in southern Yemen, a region where it has long sought influence. In exchange, Saudi Arabia’s air force would provide support for those forces against the Houthis.

Further details of Emirati involvement remain scarce. But numerous prominent Saudi and Emirati media outlets have published conciliatory commentary following the recent meeting, emphasizing the shared benefits of cooperation and calling for an end to public feuding.

The shift in tone signals an effort to sideline the December 2025 rupture in relations, which saw UAE-backed Southern Transitional Council (STC) forces capture large parts of the Hadramawt and al-Mahra provinces bordering Saudi Arabia.

The advance, which Riyadh viewed as a direct threat to its national security within its southern neighbor, triggered severe public recriminations.

It also led to a Saudi-led airstrike on a weapons shipment at Mukalla port that it said had arrived in support of the STC, and an abrupt demand for the remaining UAE forces to leave Yemen, along with the severe weakening of the STC.

That confrontation exposed competing visions for Yemen that had strained their intervention from the outset.

Although both led a war against the Houthis, known officially as Ansar Allah, starting in 2015, Riyadh backed the internationally-recognized government, while Abu Dhabi cultivated southern armed groups, including the separatist STC.

The Saudis wanted a unified government capable of defeating the Houthis, while the UAE prioritized advancing southern Yemen’s independence via the STC in a bid to gain control over ports, including Aden, which lies near the mouth of the Red Sea.

Those differences flared up in 2019, when STC and government forces fought for control of Aden, until a marriage of convenience saw Riyadh and Abu Dhabi unify these factions into a fragile power-sharing agreement.

Nevertheless, describing this simply as Saudi support for the internationally-recognized government against Emirati support for separatists would obscure both countries’ reliance on myriad local armed partners. Those relationships offer Abu Dhabi a means of re-engaging without returning its own forces to the battlefield.

The UAE is unlikely to fight the Houthis directly as it did in the previous stage of the war. The Houthis had previously struck Emirati territory, notably in 2022, showcasing the risks for the UAE, whose economy relies on projecting an image of a secure commercial oasis in an otherwise turbulent region.

And having already faced intensive Iranian missile and drone attacks since the U.S. and Israel launched their war against Iran, Abu Dhabi may be more inclined to limit its role to supporting local anti-Houthi factions, particularly given the Houthis’ markedly improved strike capabilities.

Still, even though Emirati involvement in Yemen would likely prove secretive, it could play a critical role in the coalition.

Abu Dhabi has built influence through relationships with capable local militias – including the Giants Brigades and Tarek Saleh’s National Resistance Forces – and a wider network of commercial and security interests. Although some major Emirati-backed factions merged into the Saudi-led military structures in Yemen following Abu Dhabi’s withdrawal of direct funding last year, residual command networks and personal loyalties remain intact.

Therefore, Abu Dhabi maintains significant leverage, which it can tap into by rapidly reactivating financial and logistical support. The question is whether it will use that power to boost the coalition or counter Riyadh, including by constraining its options in the south.

Indeed, the real danger is that Riyadh and Abu Dhabi will each maintain their own channels of influence and back parallel structures that end up causing fractures in territories beyond Houthi control.

Beyond geostrategic differences, there are potential ideological clashes. One longstanding source of friction is the Islamist Islah party, which is allegedly tied to the Muslim Brotherhood. Despite both governments’ hostility towards the Muslim Brotherhood, Riyadh has maintained relationships with Islah politicians within the internationally-recognized government.

Abu Dhabi, meanwhile, has seen no room for compromise. The UAE has reportedly even hired mercenaries to assassinate the faction’s leaders.

As long as Riyadh insists on working with Islah as a pragmatic means of strengthening the anti-Houthi coalition, this disagreement alone may hinder the level of support that Abu Dhabi will provide for government-backed forces.

Agreement on confronting the Houthis therefore does not necessarily extend to agreement on which Yemeni actors should be empowered.

Disagreements over who should govern Yemen could also complicate decisions about how to fight the Houthis and on what terms to negotiate. Since the U.N.-brokered ceasefire in April 2022, Riyadh has spent years seeking a negotiated exit from Yemen’s war, but the renewed Houthi attacks on Saudi territory — including deadly strikes on the Riyadh airport and attacks on oil infrastructure — have shown the limits of its containment policy, which aims to check Houthi advances without a return to full-scale war.

Regional factors matter too. Saudi Arabia has already called on Turkey, Pakistan and Egypt for defensive support against Houthi strikes, in line with the Mecca Defense Alliance, signaling that it is looking beyond its traditional reliance on the UAE.

That could deepen divisions and suggest that Riyadh increasingly views its alliance with Abu Dhabi as less essential. Meanwhile, divisions among various anti-Houthi groups remain deep. Southern factions are still divided over independence, autonomy, the distribution of power and their relationship with the rest of the country, reflecting longstanding tensions that predate Yemen’s unification in 1990.

Ultimately, any Saudi-UAE military coordination will remain fragile so long as the two Gulf powers continue to pursue conflicting endgames for Yemen.

The real test is whether any renewed cooperation yields accountable financing, coherent command structures and a political process that genuinely includes Yemen’s competing factions.

Without those elements, Riyadh and Abu Dhabi may very well end up assembling a coalition that will fight the Houthis today but crumble tomorrow, further fueling the instability that has long plagued Yemen.

item.title: The war is pushing Iran closer to Russia
item.description:
The war is pushing Iran closer to Russia Expert comment thilton.drupal 2 November 2026

A flurry of diplomatic meetings and positive statements suggest Tehran sees closer cooperation with Moscow as key to its short-term survival and long-term deterrence.

The US-Israeli war with Iran is fundamentally changing how Tehran views Russia. Moscow was previously perceived by some in Tehran as an unreliable partner that benefited disproportionately from Iran’s support. But Russia is now increasingly seen as an important partner to ensure Iran’s military survival, post-war reconstruction and long-term deterrence. 

Positive meetings

In October alone, senior Iranian and Russian officials held three high-level meetings, reflecting the growing importance both governments attach to the partnership. 

On 8 October, Iran’s president Masoud Pezeshkian met Russian president Vladimir Putin in Turkmenistan on the sidelines of regional summit meetings. They emphasized the mutual political will to deepen ties across virtually every sector, including trade and economic cooperation.

On 19 October, Russia’s foreign minister Sergei Lavrov travelled to Tehran for the first since the war began on 28 February. He met President Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Supreme National Security Council head Mohsen Rezaei. They discussed energy, transport and broader bilateral relations. The meetings emphasized the need to advance the comprehensive strategic partnership signed in January 2025, continuing economic and investment cooperation despite the challenges posed by the war.

Related work

Russia–Africa Summit: Moscow is engaging more with Africa, but its delivery is limited

After the meetings, Araghchi stated: ‘never in our history have Iran and Russia worked as closely as now.’ Pezeshkian thanked Russia for its support during the war. Security chief Rezaei also emphasized Tehran’s determination to strengthen strategic cooperation with Moscow, indicating that Iran’s security leadership also supports closer relations. 

On 27 October, Pezeshkian visited Moscow to attend the Gas Exporting Countries Forum, where he again held talks on bilateral cooperation with Putin. Pezeshkian thanked Putin for ‘backing and assistance’ in both political and economic matters. Putin said that bilateral trade increased by 10.4 per cent during the first eight months of 2026.

Putin also reaffirmed Moscow’s commitment to ongoing projects, including the Bushehr nuclear power plant. Russia’s state-owned nuclear corporation, Rosatom, announced it would increase the number of its construction workers at Bushehr to 200. Rosatom had evacuated its staff after the outbreak of the war. 

Outside of this nuclear development, the substance of these meetings was not significantly different to previous high-level exchanges. What stands out, however, is the increasingly positive tone of public statements by senior figures across Iran’s political and security establishment. This suggests a more favourable assessment of Russia’s strategic value, although it does not necessarily indicate a fundamental change in the views of all Iranian decisionmakers.

Moving beyond scepticism

This enthusiasm contrasts with earlier doubts within Tehran about the benefits of investing in Moscow as an ally. Elements of the Iranian leadership have long held a deep-seated scepticism towards Russia. 

This scepticism had grown since late 2022 as some in Tehran questioned the returns on its support for Russia’s war in Ukraine. Iran has supplied Russia with thousands of drones, including Shahed-131 and Shahed-136 models, along with other military assistance. Iran has publicly denied involvement in the conflict, but admitted it had sent drones to Russia before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and Iranian officials told Reuters months into the war that Tehran had agreed to supply more drones and missiles. 

Leaked contract documents indicate that Russia agreed to pay approximately $290,000 per drone for a bulk purchase of 2,000 Shahed-136 drones, although the extent to which these payments were completed remains unclear. Iran has also reportedly helped to establish production facilities in Russia, enabling Moscow to domestically manufacture a modified version of Iran’s Shahed-136 drone named Geran-2. 

However, influential voices in Tehran have often questioned the strategic alliance with Moscow. One former IRGC naval commander said ‘There is a view that Russia sought to drag Iran into that [Ukraine] war … so it would not be alone and the pressure of sanctions would increase on Iran.’ In 2022, the US and EU imposed additional sanctions on Iran over its sales of drones to Russia. During Lavrov’s previous visit to Tehran in February 2025, Iranian commentators warned that Moscow might use Iran as a bargaining chip in negotiations with Washington over Ukraine. 

Critics of closer relations have also argued that Russia was benefiting disproportionately from Tehran’s support, without providing comparable assistance in return. In particular, Tehran felt Russia did not significantly come to its aid during the 12-day war between Iran and Israel in June 2025. Russia failed to deliver advanced weapons systems that Iran said it had purchased before the war, such as SU-35 fighter jets.

Support for closer cooperation

The US-Israeli war appears to have prompted a reassessment of Russia’s value to Tehran. According to several reports, Russia provided Iran with intelligence on US military positions, satellite imagery for targeting, and weapons components. It is difficult to assess the real battlefield impact of Russian support. However, despite President Donald Trump’s statement that Moscow and Beijing have not been helping Tehran, the evidence suggests otherwise.

Such support is likely to have strengthened the position of those within Iran’s security establishment who have long advocated closer ties with Moscow. For this group, who were supported by the late former president, Ebrahim Raisi, the war has vindicated their longstanding argument that closer cooperation with Russia could deliver tangible strategic benefits. These include helping Iran circumvent sanctions, overcoming diplomatic isolation and countering Western pressure. 

The increasingly positive statements from senior political officials such as Pezeshkian and Araghchi suggests that support for closer cooperation with Russia is becoming more widespread across the Iranian political spectrum, including among those once sceptical of close alignment with Moscow.  

As Tehran prioritizes military survival, deterrence, and reconstruction in the coming months, closer cooperation with Russia will likely be increasingly seen as a strategic necessity rather than merely as a means of circumventing sanctions and resisting Western pressure. The partnership is acquiring a more immediate security rationale, serving both Iran’s current military requirements and its longer-term strategic objectives.

Consequences

In the short term, technical assistance and weapons components could help Iran withstand the conflict by sustaining capabilities degraded by months of fighting. Russian expertise could help Tehran rebuild its air defences, missile infrastructure, and defence industry. Russian intelligence could help Iranian forces track US military assets and inform operational decisions. 

Russian support will be particularly valuable in the event of renewed military escalation. It could improve Iran’s ability to anticipate attacks, preserve its military capabilities and impose costs on its adversaries. However, it is unlikely to fundamentally alter the balance of power in Iran’s favour.

In the medium term, assuming the war comes to an end, Iran-Russia cooperation will likely continue with the aim of rebuilding Iran’s military capabilities. This would likely focus on air defence, drones and missile technology. 

While Russia’s capacity to meet Iran’s demands will remain constrained by its war in Ukraine and pressure on its defence industry, even selective transfers of technology and expertise would help Tehran address its vulnerabilities and accelerate the restoration of its deterrent capabilities. For example, Russia could provide replacement components for the S-300 missile defence system as well as electronic warfare technology.

In the longer term, the most consequential outcome could be the institutionalization of military cooperation between Iran and Russia. Iranian policymakers will remain wary of Russia’s tendency to prioritize its own interests and the absence of a binding security guarantee. But the relationship is likely to become increasingly central in future military planning, procurement and defence-industrial cooperation. This will likely increase Iran’s ability to withstand US military and economic pressure, albeit without being a game changer in the balance of power.

The war may not have transformed Russia into a reliable security guarantor for Iran, but it could make Moscow a more enduring component of Tehran’s security strategy. This will ensure the partnership is harder to reverse, no matter who is in power.

Britain's elites are in hysterics over looming 'war' with Russia
item.description:
British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting recently said the U.K. has 1000 days to be “ready with our allies to fight and win.” The enemy is obvious: Russia. The catch: London doesn’t have the cash to fight, and ordinary folk aren’t interested.

This latest reminder that war with our Slavic foes is imminent is vague and unspecified, and frankly tedious. As the Wall Street Journal pointed out nearly a year ago, “rarely a week goes by now without a European government, military or security chief making a grim speech warning the public that they are headed toward a potential war with Russia.”

Streeting is simply the latest to join the chorus. Earlier in October, he advised British people to stock up on tinned food and bottled water in case of an emergency, a suggestion he has since repeated.

Yet a gap is growing between this war readiness rhetoric and the reality of public finances in Britain. It is evident that the government has little fiscal headroom to increase defense spending rapidly to the NATO target of 3.5% of GDP by 2035. In his annual budget statement last week, Chancellor (and former Defense Secretary) John Healy said the 3% target would be reached “in the next Parliament,” which could be as late as 2034. Current spending plans suggest U.K. defense won’t go beyond 2.7% this decade.

We can’t afford to expand our army which, at 73,500 troops, is already at its smallest since 1823, according to MoD data. There are more than 700,000 Russian troops in Ukraine alone. When discussions kicked off in March 2025 about a “coalition of the willing” peacekeeping force for Ukraine, the U.K. armed forces were considered “too stretched” to contribute without cutting back operations elsewhere. A British MP and member of the U.K. parliamentary defense select committee told me we would struggle to put 10,000 troops on the field.

Nevertheless, a concerted campaign appears underway to soften Brits up for the fight. This past weekend, the Spectator put out a piece calling for the reintroduction of mandatory National Service for 18-year-olds. “What we need is a resilient, hardened and capable population, ready for the tough times ahead,” wrote Ted Jeffery. “Not a country with 10 million working-age people on benefits.”

No one talks about how to pay for schemes like this, except, one assumes, to cut back on benefits. Herein lies the guns or butter faultline in British political discussion, which you can also witness in Germany and in France. The state should cut back on public services such as welfare and instead spend money on defense and war readiness.

The protests and riots that have rocked France are not driven by concerns about the risk of war, but rather about the dilapidation of the school system. This past weekend has also seen riots across Germany about the cost of living. Former German Foreign Minister Annalena Baerbock’s suggestion that she would back Ukraine “no matter what voters think” helps explain why increasing numbers of Germans are turning to parties such as Alternative für Deutschland (AfD).

Foreign policy starts and ends at home. Ordinary folk spend little time thinking about foreign policy and assume that their governments will focus on domestic concerns. That gives elected leaders considerable scope to cut a dash on the world stage in the face of public indifference. However, it does not offer carte blanche to put foreign issues first.

In Britain, the public doesn’t appear remotely interested in fighting a foreign war. A recent poll by Ipsos found that 48% of Britons would not agree to fight “under any circumstances” while only 36% might be willing.

Indeed, the most interesting observation was that the age group most willing was the over 55s. This cohort might get its chance as last week the government announced it had updated its policies determining that reservists up to 65 years of age could be reactivated "to strengthen UK readiness as global threats continue to grow."

The British Foreign Policy Group’s 2026 Survey also indicated that 52% of Britons would be unwilling, and 58% unable, to fight, with a similar tilt towards the older generation.

The government has made some effort to persuade its citizens to change their minds. In late October, the Head of the Army, Sir Roland Walker, warned that “our citizens have got to consent to sacrifices to prioritize defense and security.” This follows on from the highly publicized remarks on GB News that pro-Russian (read pro-peace) voices should be locked up and conscription should be introduced.

The latter was pure bloviation. The former, an incitement by a serving military officer to put conscription into practice. This was leapt upon by historian Peter Hitchens, who wrote that it was not for serving military officers “to put the case for sacrifices by the voting public. Nor was it for him to tell politicians to explain this to the public.” I heartily agree.

British ministers and pundits never explain where we might meet the Russians in battle after we’ve been press-ganged and put into uniforms. Anyone who believes they are going to romp all the way across Europe and cross the channel to meet us here must be a fantasist. That means we either go into Ukraine, which we have steadfastly avoided doing since 2014, or we send our troops to a NATO country that is attacked, despite the lack of evidence that Russia has any intention of launching such an endeavor.

A more credible, less expensive and less dangerous approach would be to engage in diplomacy to put an end to conflict, rather than allowing it to fester and worsen. With a government too poor to grow the army and with a population unwilling to fight, Britain nevertheless clings to its refusal to talk and engage in diplomacy. At the recent G20 Foreign Ministers’ meeting in Atlanta, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, beside a grinning Foreign Minister Radek Sikorski of Poland, used the plenary to lambast Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and declare “you are not winning the war”.

A planned family photo, where the ministers all stand together, was canceled because the Brits and Europeans didn’t want to be in shot with Lavrov. Further proof, sadly, that statecraft in Britain and Europe today resembles a bunch of 10-year-olds squabbling in the schoolyard.

The Coming Age of Robotic Warfare
item.description:
A battalion of armed robots moves against a unit of soldiers, aiming to seize territory. In the ensuing battle, the robots open fire, communicate with one another and change tactics as needed. Air cover is provided by uncrewed drones; logistical support and supplies are delivered by a separate team of robots. Territory is taken, prisoners captured. When the battle is over, the attacking side has lost several drones and robots, but no human beings have been killed or wounded.

Science fiction? Hardly. Some elements in this scenario – unmanned aerial cover and logistical support – are already commonplace in Ukraine. So are small-scale robot-led military actions. And experts say the other piece – robots leading major battlefield operations – is coming soon.

Ukraine's ex-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who led a warp-speed campaign to bring an “Army of Drones” to the battlefield, has launched what he calls a “Manhattan Project” to build an “Army of Robots.”

“The goal of the Robot Army is to save human lives,” Fedorov said in a recent presentation. “Robots should perform the most dangerous work so that our soldiers return home.”

“The main question for 2027 is not whether Ukraine will have an army of robots – it already does,” said Morgan, the commander of a Special Operations Group in the DIU (Defense Intelligence of Ukraine), who goes by his call name.

“The question is how quickly we can scale it up, and hand over to robots more of the tasks that people perform today at the risk of their own lives.”

It’s a brave new world of warfighting, and beyond its life-saving promise, it raises questions about non-human decision-making, and how widely and quickly AI-guided robots will displace the world’s soldiers.

“The premise has to be that there will be human control,” Lt. Gen. Jack Shanahan (Ret.), who served as the first director of the Defense Department’s Joint Artificial Intelligence Center, told The Cipher Brief.

“What we have to figure out is where, when and how that control gets applied. I do not want to see machines deciding…to do something that the humans never anticipated.”

Major Yabchanka’s Journey

When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Oleksandr Yabchanka was a combat medic; today, he commands an unmanned systems platoon for the “Da Vinci Wolves” battalion, and specializes in what he calls “the robotization of combat processes.”

“The route a robot covers today is one that people would previously have had to cover,” Major Yabchanka told The Cipher Brief. “In our conditions, that would mean an extremely high risk of being hit. Robots take that risk upon themselves.”

Nearly every Ukrainian military unit now uses AI-guided robots, or UGVs (unmanned ground vehicles), for a range of mundane but dangerous tasks. Yabchanka described a supply chain that begins with human soldiers in rear positions who hand off ammunition, food and other supplies to UGVs for the proverbial last mile to the front. Robots repair cables and antennas, transfer munitions, and help armored vehicles that are stuck in the mud. And increasingly, they’ve been evacuating wounded soldiers.

“This is one of the most difficult operations, often carried out under intense fire,” Morgan, the Special Operations commander, told The Cipher Brief. “When robotic systems are used for evacuation, the risk is significantly reduced for service members who would otherwise have to go out to help their wounded comrades.” He believes that ground robots have already saved tens of thousands of lives.

“Imagine having to carry a wounded person ten kilometers,” Major Yabchanka said. “It takes a long time, it’s physically exhausting, and once detected, the evacuation team becomes a priority target. We risk losing both the wounded soldier and those who go to save him. That is why we hand this work over to UGVs.”

Ukraine's Defense Ministry reported in September that UGVs had carried out 112,000 logistics and casualty-evacuation missions this year.

“Many of the (scenarios) are no longer science fiction,” Major Yabchanka said. “The question is not so much whether an army of robots is possible, but how quickly we can bring these technologies to the required level of reliability, integrate them into combat processes and ensure their mass use.”

Robot soldiers that think

The holy grail in this robotic evolution is full-scale offensive operations. Call that Mykhailo Fedorov’s dream.

For the moment, battlefield decisions are still made by humans. Those casualty evacuations are overseen by a human operator; and no large “units” of robots have gone into battle alone.

But in small ways, Fedorov’s dream is already a reality.

The New York Times reported on a battle in the Kharkiv region featuring robotic vehicles which advanced on a Russian position – “little green wagons” that “looked like something you might buy at a garden store to move bags of soil.” Each vehicle carried 66 pounds of explosives, and as they neared the Russian troops, an aerial drone dropped a bomb and one of the robots blew itself up.

Two Russian soldiers soon emerged from a trench with a sign that read “We want to surrender.”

In other words, a robot-led attack had resulted in the capture of Russian prisoners. “It is better to throw in metal than people,” Lt. Mykola Zinkevych, who commanded the attack, told the Times. “Human life is precious, and robots don’t bleed.”

More recently, in Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi in the Donbas, UGVs were dropped by aerial drones deep into Russian lines; the robots then attacked Russian positions. As one of Vivaldi’s commanders, who goes by “Darwin,” told The Cipher Brief, his men would establish a defense line and then wait “until artillery, flying drones and robots do their work, and then go in again.” Darwin said his corps was the first to demonstrate such coordination between autonomous and human elements.

David Kirichenko, an Associate Research Fellow at the Henry Jackson Society, said Vivaldi had demonstrated “the inexorable erosion of the usefulness of humans in direct contact with the enemy.”

In another recent milestone, Ukraine’s "Lava" Unmanned Systems Regiment carried out what it said was the world’s first combat logistics mission utilizing an AI-driven ground robot without human supervision. The Defense Ministry said its robot navigated 93 percent of a roughly 12-mile route; a human operator stepped in only for a one-mile stretch where the terrain differed from what mapping software had suggested.

Fedorov’s “Manhattan Project,” which he unveiled at a conference in Lviv in late September, would take all this to scale – battalions of “humanoid robots” that are given a mission and are able to adjust tactics in mid-battle. Swarms of aerial drones have already shown this capability; as Lt. Gen. Shanahan noted, “we’re talking about drone swarms on the ground as opposed to in the air.” Fedorov says his “Army of Robots” is a logical evolution in the autonomous weapons space, and a way to address Ukraine’s manpower shortage.

“We want to eventually substitute our infantry with these robots,” he said.

Fedorov’s plans are supported by a new consortium that includes outside investors including Palantir CEO Alex Karp. In a recent interview, Fedorov said the project had attracted more than 800 applications from companies, engineers, designers and programmers.

As with nearly all military innovation in Ukraine, the “Army of Robots” time horizon is ambitious. Fedorov’s presentation included an initial six-month phase culminating when a “humanoid robot” kills its first Russian soldier; within a year, he said, robots will be ready to conduct major coordinated assaults on their own.

“We don’t have enough time,” Fedorov told the Lviv conference. “We need to achieve these results as soon as possible.”

The Pentagon’s Push

Ukraine is now the widely-recognized global testing ground for new military technology, the home to what Cipher Brief expert and former CIA Director Gen. David Petraeus has referred to as “tomorrow's technology for today's wars.”

With this in mind, American manufacturers have sent prototypes of robotic soldiers to Ukraine. In June, San Francisco-based Foundation Future Industries said it had dispatched its Phantom Mk1 robots to Ukraine for battlefield testing. Foundation CEO Sankaet Pathak said he was “convinced the technology is reaching a level where it can replace jobs that are dangerous for humans to perform, and if you can do that, it’s the highest net good you can create out of all applications of robotics.”

Meanwhile, the U.S. and other countries are escalating efforts to boost robotic capabilities within their militaries. In late September, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the creation of an Autonomous Warfare Command, and called on all the services to accelerate their autonomous and robotic capabilities.

“We will fuse procurement with operations at scale,” Hegseth said, “and allow warfighters and engineers and entrepreneurs to learn, adapt, and rapidly iterate on their domain.”

“What we’re beginning to see with the U.S military is an increasing emphasis on autonomous systems on the ground side, the sea side and the air side,” Lt. Gen. Shanahan said. “I sense a palpable sense of urgency that I didn’t feel a couple of years ago.”

Experts say the urgency is driven by Ukraine’s successes as well as the possibility of conflict with China. China is developing sophisticated military robotic systems of its own, helped by an already-strong commercial robotics and electronics sector. Recently China showcased quadrupedal ground robots, or “robotic wolves,” which experts say are designed to cover rough and mountainous terrain. Beijing’s broader military strategy emphasizes “intelligentized warfare”; integrating AI, robotics, and data networks into combat operations.

Lt. Gen. Shanahan says such integration will be critical for the U.S. as it boosts its autonomous systems.

“Technically, it’s doable pretty quickly,” Shanahan said. “Organizationally, and the integration piece of it, these are hard things to work through.”

Risks and limitations

Questions abound about the future of robotic armies – not least, their reliability, mobility and ability to react under fire. “Humanoid robots” are expensive, mechanically complicated and – for the moment at least – far less sophisticated than conventional ground vehicles and drones.

“You still need to take ground and hold it to end a war, and both sides have to agree the war is over,” Shanahan said. “You can’t do that with drones on the ground...At some point you will need to end up putting humans on the ground to hold ground or push back.”

Among practical concerns, experts list communications, cost and coordination.

An operator cannot continuously control a robot if the adversary jams its radio links; Major Yabchanka has seen his UGVs frequently disabled by Russian electronic jamming. “For more complex autonomous functions,” he said, “more and more computing has to happen on board the robotic system itself, without depending on an external server or a continuous communication link. This requires additional computing power, sensors and power supply. All of this increases cost.”

In terms of coordination, large “units” of deployed robots must avoid collisions, particularly in a dynamic battlefield. As with other AI-driven systems, experts say repeated battlefield tests will help iron out such problems.

The most profound questions involve the human element. Will human beings remain in control of missions once they are launched? Will robot soldiers identify potential targets? And will robots or humans authorize engagement?

“We get so caught up in technology itself, we forget what the most important piece of it is,” Shanahan said. “How are you going to fight with it? What’s your operating concept? What’s your organizational design, for bringing in all these ground systems? Where do you want to put the humans, where do you want to put the machines?”

Shanahan raised one specific nightmare scenario: a robot unit that collectively “decides” that its mission is best served by striking a civilian target that no human has authorized.

“You could see this robot out there with agentic capability, deciding that the quickest way to end the war is not to hit this thing that the human wants it to hit, but to hit that hospital over there because the enemy will back down once 500 civilians are killed in a hospital off the battlefield,” Shanahan said. “That’s a catastrophe in the making.”

Even frontline commanders in Ukraine, who crave every technological edge they can get, share such concerns.

“Questions that once seemed like fiction are now becoming entirely practical,” Major Yabchanka said. “Today, in most of the systems we work with, the decision to use lethal force remains with the operator. But technology is already moving toward a point where that decision could be handed over to a machine…We could end up in a situation where the decision to kill a human being gradually ceases to be a human decision. This is a very dangerous stage of technological development, and humanity should not rush toward it.”

Morgan, the special operations commander, shares these concerns. But he also calls Ukraine’s AI-driven robots “one of our enormous advantages over Russia.”

Yabchanka agrees. “Robotization is not just a new technology,” he said. “It is our competitive advantage and one of the main paths to victory over an enemy with far greater manpower. This is not just a matter of technological progress. I am convinced that this is how we can win this war.”

item.title: Fire Base Australia: Can America’s Southern Base Sustain a Pacific War?
item.description:
American access to Australian bases is only as valuable as Australia’s ability to keep them operating under attack. For Washington, expanding military cooperation raises an operational question: can Australia sustain an American campaign while defending its own territory, infrastructure and population?

For Canberra, the corresponding question is whether investment in national resilience is keeping pace with Australia’s growing usefulness to American operations. Both governments need convincing answers before a regional crisis turns access arrangements into wartime demands.

The benefits are considerable. Australian facilities offer strategic depth, logistical support and opportunities to disperse forces. Australia gains access to American capabilities, intelligence and interoperability. Their wartime value, however, depends on protection, sustainment and the host country’s continued ability to function.

The 2026 Iran war offers a warning. Despite America’s regional military presence, Gulf partners suffered casualties, damage and disruption from Iranian attacks. The lesson is not that every incoming weapon must be intercepted. It is that defending individual facilities and sustaining the country around them are different tasks.

Australia differs substantially from the Gulf states. Nevertheless, an adversary could seek to weaken an American campaign by imposing costs on its Australian support network. A base might remain operational while disruption to surrounding energy, transport and civilian services progressively reduces its usefulness.

Australia could face three simultaneous responsibilities: supporting American operations, contributing combat forces and defending its homeland. Aircraft assigned to coalition missions might also be needed to protect Australian approaches. Maritime forces could face competing demands to support forward operations and secure essential supply routes. Fuel, munitions and maintenance capacity would serve all three responsibilities.

These tensions matter directly to Washington. Disruption could reduce sortie generation, delay replenishment and constrain repairs. Requests for additional protection could divert American forces from other missions. Civilian hardship could generate political pressure over the scale or conditions of continued Australian support.

This is a planning problem, not a prediction that Australia would abandon its ally. Alliance planning should make such pressure difficult to exploit.

The ANZUS Treaty provides a commitment to meet common danger through each country’s constitutional processes. It does not allocate the forces, stockpiles or repair capacity needed to sustain Australia under attack. Those arrangements require practical agreement.

Canberra carries substantial responsibility. It cannot expand its supporting role while assuming Washington will supply whatever protection becomes necessary. Australia’s 2026 National Defence Strategy emphasizes greater self-reliance, industrial resilience and civil preparedness. The test is whether implementation can sustain national defense and alliance operations simultaneously.

Washington must likewise distinguish access from assured capacity. American forces operating from Australia may have missions elsewhere; their presence should not automatically be counted as an equivalent addition to Australian territorial defense. Reassigning them would carry consequences for the wider campaign.

The Wartime Planning Dilemma

Consider a Taiwan conflict later this decade in which the United States intervenes and Australia provides access, logistical support and a limited combat contribution while defending itself. This is a planning scenario, not a forecast. Proposed facilities must be assessed separately from capabilities already available.

Northern airfields, including Darwin and Tindal, could support aircraft rotations, staging, refueling and maintenance. Upgrades at Tindal to accommodate American bombers increase its potential utility. But aircraft parking capacity does not determine sustained combat output. Fuel distribution, munitions handling, maintenance personnel and runway repair would govern how frequently aircraft could operate.

Southern Australia offers additional depth. Reported plans for a Marine Corps prepositioning facility in Victoria, expected to reach full capacity in 2028, illustrate the value of storing equipment away from northern operating locations. Distance can reduce exposure to some threats while increasing transport requirements and replenishment times.

Such facilities also require planning with surrounding communities. Targeting exposure, hazardous fuel and ammunition storage, and pressure on civilian roads, utilities and emergency services must all be assessed. Local preparedness is part of operational resilience.

In Western Australia, HMAS Stirling could support submarine operations and sustainment. Its contribution would depend on qualified personnel, specialist facilities and available components, rather than port access alone. Joint facilities, including Pine Gap’s intelligence and missile-warning functions and Harold E. Holt’s submarine communications, add capabilities whose disruption could affect operations far beyond Australia.

The threat should be assessed across three overlapping tiers. These describe the expanding scope of disruption, not a predictable escalation sequence.

Tier one: military capability. Attacks on airfields, naval facilities, logistics installations or communications could reduce operational output without destroying entire bases. Planners should test combinations of physical attack, cyber disruption and sabotage. Concentrating essential functions at a few locations creates dependencies that dispersal, hardening, redundancy and rapid repair must address.

The relevant measure is how much military activity survives and how quickly lost capacity returns. An intact runway offers limited value if fuel cannot reach aircraft or maintenance systems are unavailable.

Tier two: the civilian systems sustaining military operations. Electricity, telecommunications, commercial ports, roads and fuel distribution connect military facilities to the national economy. Their disruption could constrain operations even where bases escape direct attack. Several modest interruptions could combine into a serious loss of capacity.

Fuel illustrates the problem. Canberra’s 2026 fuel-security package includes a A$3.2 billion government reserve and measures intended to lift diesel and aviation-fuel reserves to 50 days. This is an important investment, but a national stockholding target does not establish endurance under wartime consumption or guarantee delivery to the facilities needing it.

Tier three: national endurance and political decision-making. Prolonged disruption could place military requirements in competition with hospitals, food distribution, civilian transport and essential industry. Shipping interruptions could compound domestic damage. The resulting hardship could become a means of coercion, whether or not civilian suffering was the initial purpose of an attack.

Deliberate attacks on population centers would represent an additional, grave contingency. They are not necessary for this tier to emerge: disruption to shared infrastructure could already produce substantial civilian harm. Planning must therefore include essential-service continuity, emergency communications and support for affected communities, alongside military recovery.

Across all three tiers, the central question is the same: how much pressure can Australia absorb while sustaining its agreed contribution?

Turning Access into Endurance

The answer requires decisions before hostilities. Both governments should establish which functions each facility can sustain, for how long, and under what assumptions about replenishment and damage. Planned capacity should enter campaign calculations only when it is available, staffed and exercised.

The United States Studies Centre has recommended prioritizing the “five R’s” of logistics—refuel, rearm, resupply, repair and revive—through the Combined Logistics Sustainment and Maintenance Enterprise announced at the 2021 Australia–U.S. Ministerial Consultations. This provides an existing foundation for stronger sustainment arrangements.

The additional requirement is to test those arrangements against simultaneous homeland-defense and civilian-continuity demands. Logistics cooperation alone cannot settle who protects facilities or who receives scarce resources.

First, the allies should agree protection responsibilities and procedures for allocating scarce aircraft, fuel, munitions, transport and repair capacity. Australian homeland defense, Australian combat deployments and American operations cannot each assume first call on the same resources. Governments must retain decision-making authority, but the trade-offs should be understood beforehand.

Second, investment should address the dependencies that most constrain sustained output: alternative distribution routes, dispersed reserves, repair teams, replacement components and resilient communications. Additional operating capacity should be matched by the capacity to protect, supply and restore it.

Third, joint exercises should test concurrent disruption across military installations and civilian networks. State governments, infrastructure operators and emergency services should participate where relevant. Exercises should measure sustained output and recovery times under delayed replenishment, rather than merely demonstrate that forces can deploy.

Neither government needs to disclose classified plans to make these priorities visible in budgets and preparedness programs.

A resilient Australia gives Washington more dependable operational options and reduces emergency reinforcement demands. An exposed Australia could require additional protection precisely when American forces are most heavily committed elsewhere.

The alliance’s southern base will be judged by what it can sustain under pressure. Australian resilience must therefore be treated as an essential input to American campaign planning, with responsibilities agreed, resources funded and recovery exercised before war begins.
