item.title: The Hidden Cost of America’s War With Iran
item.description:
“The [U.S. Naval Support Activity Bahrain] base and Fifth Fleet headquarters have been rendered largely inoperable for their original functions, with repairs estimated at $400 million… Chief of Naval Operations Admiral Daryl Caudle and other senior defense officials stated that the Navy will not return to full normal operations at the Bahrain facility anytime soon…Because the Juffair surrounding area [to the U.S. Bahrain Navy facilities] is considered unsafe, [U.S. Navy] major logistical and port-call operations have been rerouted over 2,000 miles away to the Naval Support Facility Diego Garcia and other alternative hubs, causing significant resupply delays.”

That is an excerpt from a 19-page Congressional Budget Office (CBO) report titled, Estimating the Cost of Combat Operations Against Iran, sent to Congress September 15.

I read the now-seven-week-old CBO report last week, and was surprised at how much new-to-me information it contained about the early days of the Iran war, and particularly Tehran’s early destruction of U.S. military infrastructure which, up-to-recently, had not had much publicity in this country.

For example, although the U.S. attacks along with Israel on Iran began before dawn February 28, 2026, there apparently was a lack of expectation for the size of Iran counterattacks with missiles and drones that actually took place later that same day, February 28, in Bahrain and at other U.S. bases in Qatar, Kuwait, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates.

And while the White House and Pentagon repeatedly have described the destruction U.S. and Israeli forces have done to Iran’s military, there has been as almost no mention of what was happening to the U.S. facilities.

In mid-September, the Defense Department (DoD) Inspector General (IG), as Lead IG, released a report on Operation Epic Fury (OEF) -- the war against Iran. The IG report found that “Iranian strikes damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan during the conflict,” as of June 30, 2026, and the DoD had “$3.7 billion in equipment losses, but [that] does not include costs for infrastructure repairs.”

The IG report later noted it “did not include the cost of military construction for damaged infrastructure in its estimate because [DoD] has not determined what its future posture will be in the region, how it will construct its bases, and what percentage of the construction costs Allies and partners will contribute.”

On the other hand, the IG report did say “damage to U.S. embassies, consulates, and other diplomatic facilities had already cost the U.S. approximately $184 million.”

I should point out that the CBO September report, sent to Congress one day after the IG report was released, noted that DoD had failed to provide to it, the CBO, with an estimate on the cost of the damage to U.S. bases and facilities.

In fact, there still has yet to be any publicly-released official DoD estimate of the cost of damage to U.S. military bases and facilities based on Iran’s attacks.

However, Iran attacks in those first days of the war continued in a scale and duration that appeared to have taken the U.S. government by surprise. For example, it was not until March 2, the third day after attacks began, before the Navy and the State Department ordered the evacuation of dependents from Bahrain.

The September CBO report said, “Military families and non-essential personnel were evacuated [from Bahrain] in March 2026, and remain displaced across temporary housing, awaiting the eventual retrieval of personal belongings left behind…[and] Evacuated families have faced added strain as military leadership noted that temporary evacuation financial support is scheduled to conclude on November 30, 2026, even though shipping personal effects is expected to take several more months.”

Also indicating a surprise from Iran’s military response, the DoD’s IG report noted, “Prior to OEF, Bahrain had been U.S. Navy Central’s main logistics hub to sustain operations in the Persian Gulf region, USCENTCOM [U.S. Central Command] said. During major combat operations, Iran targeted Bahrain with [drones] and ballistic missile strikes. USCENTCOM stated that it initially shifted naval sustainment resources from Bahrain to alternate hubs.”

The IG Report added, “The establishment of adequate naval bases and support ports posed significant challenges before and during OEF, arising from complexities and due to uncertainties with host nation access permissions to utilize ports for fleet resupply, USCENTCOM said.”

For example, the need to shift logistics support and infrastructure to Diego Garcia added 14-to-18 days for transporting material by sea, according to the IG report.

As for the U.S. Combined Air and Space Operations Center (CAOC) at Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, the Air Force had since 2019 periodically conducted tests and temporary shifts of its operations to Shaw Air Force Base in South Carolina to demonstrate distributed command-and-control capabilities and reduced reliance on a single point of failure.

As reported in June by Air and Space Forces Magazine, personnel were transferred away from Al Udeid before February 28. Therefore, when Iran weapons struck the COAC facility at Al Udeid Air Base in the early days of the war, operations were already being run out of Shaw Air Force Base.

Then, there is the already publicized, but apparently un-planned, heavy use of both offensive and defensive U.S. weaponry caused by the Iran war.

For example, the September CBO report estimated, “The cost to replace the munitions expended through August 1, 2026, is $21.7 billion: $7.3 billion for the land-attack cruise missiles, $13.1 billion for the missile defense interceptors, and $1.2 billion for other munitions. Replacing those munitions has been the largest single component of the costs incurred by DoD during the conflict.”

CBO estimated that it “would probably take at least five years” to replace certain interceptors even at an increased rate of production.

An October 5, Congressional Research Service (CRS) report, U.S. Military Operations Against Iran’s Missile and Nuclear Programs, raises another point worth considering -- whether the Trump planners understood the difficulty they faced in trying to disarm Iran.

The CRS report noted that President Trump on February 28, listed among the OEF’s objectives was destroying Iran’s missiles, and “[razing] their missile industry to the ground.”

However, as CRS reported following the initial U.S./Israeli attacks, “DIA [the Defense Intelligence Agency] assessed in April 2026 that Iran ‘retains thousands of missiles and one-way attack UAVs [drones] that can threaten U.S. and partner forces throughout the region, despite degradations to its capabilities from both attrition and expenditure.’”

CRS also reported articles that said “that Iran may have begun rebuilding military infrastructure, restoring access to missile bases, and resuming missile production using stockpiled components. An Iranian official reportedly asserted in August that Iran has sufficient ‘stockpiles in our underground missile and drone cities’ to enable continued production.”

The CRS report suggested Congress consider directing the Pentagon to produce an “annual report on military power of Iran,” along with a public version of that report.

While dealing with public reporting, I must note the odd way DoD has been handling public disclosure of U.S. dead and wounded since February 28, a system clearly designed to lower the numbers.

Instead of having one category, there are two – one for the period February 28-to-July 6, covering OEF with 15 deaths and 417 wounded; the second from July 7-to-present in a second category, “overseas operations,” which lists eight deaths and 448 wounded.

The Trump administration rationale was that a temporary ceasefire or memorandum of understanding was reached to end OEF and that fighting resumed on July 7, after the earlier ceasefire collapsed.

However, as Stars and Stripes reported last Thursday, “The Pentagon has revised the number of U.S. troops who have died during operations related to the war against Iran to 23… Additionally, 865 American service members have been wounded.”

Now we are in a period where President Trump has threatened, after today’s elections, to renew attacks on Iran. He has amassed a battle force that could carry it out. He has also warned allies in the region it may be coming.

The State Department has ordered nonessential government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia and made staffing adjustments or family departures across several diplomatic missions in the Middle East.

But as I have indicated above, Iran, which has the largest armed forces in the region, has a capability to strike back, whether the Pentagon acknowledges that or not.

Iran has developed a defense industry and its own military capabilities, including extensive underground facilities, and dispersal of munitions inventories.

The volume of U.S. offensive and defensive ammunition used so far against Iran show that any U.S. renewing of attacks to force Tehran to accept Washington’s terms, would not be a day or two operation.

And perhaps just as important to think about -- given what Ukraine has shown -- explosive drones can be launched toward targets thousands of miles away, showing no country is completely safe, no matter how far its borders are from the enemy.

item.title: China and its trading partners are moving towards an economic peace. But it is a fragile one
item.description:
China and its trading partners are moving towards an economic peace. But it is a fragile one Expert comment thilton.drupal 3 November 2026

Beijing appears to have embraced economic stability in its relations with the US and the EU. But serious challenges over its currency and export model remain.

In a world full of geopolitical tension and war, it is worth pausing to consider the few signs of hope that have emerged these last few months in China’s relations with the US and the EU. 

Last month’s deal between Beijing and the EU to limit Europe’s imports of plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) is the most recent notable example. It represents an easing of trade tension and could help to defuse the threat of some very hostile trade tools that the French and German governments are now willing to deploy. 

This EU-China agreement also comes in the context of President Xi and President Trump agreeing to a period of ‘constructive strategic stability’ during Trump’s visit to China in May. While this apparent embrace of stability is welcome, China’s economic relations with its global trading partners remain contentious.

Self-serving stabilization

China has some very good reasons of its own to seek a period of stabilization. Just about the one thing that the US, the EU and many parts of the Global South can all agree on, these days, is their shared view that China should import more and export less. Beijing is immensely lucky that its trading partners can’t turn that common view into a common policy, and so they remain entirely uncoordinated in their response to China’s rapidly increasing share of the global market for manufactured goods. Beijing should worry that this luck may run out, and so it makes sense for the authorities there to offer some help. 

Related work

‘China shock 2.0’ and Europe’s industrial future

China’s reaction to the Hormuz crisis is another example of the ‘strategic reasonableness’ that Beijing seems to have adopted. China reduced its oil imports very sharply after Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz in March and threatened the world with the loss of some 12 million barrels per day of oil that couldn’t find alternative routes out of the region. In June this year, China’s oil imports were down by about 5 million barrels a day. This reduced stress in the world’s oil market, which both supported economic activity and helped minimize global inflationary pressures.

It should go without saying that self-interest was at work here. China’s intensely export-oriented growth model requires Beijing to make sure that the chokepoint leverage that it is amassing through its manufacturing dominance doesn’t lead to a catastrophic loss of trust on the part of its trading partners. And at a more basic level, China’s economic model requires its customers to stay afloat. Whatever Beijing can do to stabilize global demand conditions, it should do. And that’s not to mention the chance that rising populism in the West might take on a more explicitly anti-China hue in the future.

Fragility

It has to be said, though, that this stabilization is very fragile. For example, China’s agreement to limit its exports of PHEVs to Europe, albeit through a WTO-compliant ‘safeguard measure,’ runs several risks. One is that China’s other trading partners might wonder why Beijing offered export restraint to the EU but not them, potentially leading them to push for their own arrangements.

And within the EU, there seems to be a strong sense that now Beijing has agreed to restrain vehicles exports, the same kind of pressure could be applied to sectors like pharmaceuticals, chemicals and machinery. China’s tolerance for this might be very limited.

Moreover, Europe and China’s other trading partners have ‘whack-a-mole’ problem when it comes to Chinese manufactured exports. The main reason that a rise in PHEV exports became so visible is thanks to the tariffs that the EU imposed on battery electric vehicles two years ago: China simply boosted its exports of PHEVs which weren’t subject to the tariffs. Now that these will be constrained, it probably won’t be long before another kind of manufactured exports surge next.

Currency concerns

Another reason to curb one’s enthusiasm is the way in which the debate about global trade imbalances is likely to evolve.  

Beijing’s commitment to its manufacturing-led growth model seems, for the time being, unshakeable. What’s more likely is that China will agree to let its currency strengthen. 

Last month, France and Germany made it clear in their unofficial ‘non-paper’ on trade that an appreciation of the renminbi would be a tolerable substitute in the short term for a more meaningful economic rebalancing of the economy that would boost China’s spending on imports. More pressure on China might grow when the US Treasury publishes its next report on potential ‘currency manipulators’ early next year. 

It is difficult to argue against the idea that the renminbi remains highly undervalued. CF40, a distinguished Chinese economics think-tank, recently suggested that the underlying equilibrium exchange rate of the renminbi against the US dollar – adjusting for the fact that the cost of living in China is much lower – is around 2.5 CNY per USD. The current market exchange rate is just below 6.7.

In this respect, though, China’s trading partners should be careful what they wish for. A more expensive renminbi will inevitably boost inflationary pressures among China’s trading partners. The European Central Bank has shown how cheap imports from China have kept goods inflation more moderate than it would otherwise be. At a time when anxiety about inflation is especially acute, given the surge in prices seen since the Iran war started in February, a renminbi-induced inflation shock in Europe and the US may not be very welcome.

‘Safe’ FDI

Economic relations between China and its trading partners in the EU and the US suffer from a familiar security dilemma: my pursuit of security leaves you feeling less secure, and vice versa. 

The most hopeful way out of this might be for everyone to agree that China should increase its flow of ‘safe’ foreign direct investment (FDI) to the rest of the world.

This issue is now at the centre of talks in Europe about the European Commission’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act. Bigger FDI flows would help to lower China’s trade surplus by generating production in host countries, along with all the benefits of local job creation, technology transfer and tax revenues. 

China has a long-term incentive to park industrial assets offshore, not least because they will generate a flow of cross-border investment income in the future.  

Finding a way to increase China’s FDI flow to Europe without causing conniptions about national security risks is a worthy task. Set against the $350 billion trade deficit the EU will run with China this year, China’s FDI annual inflows of around $10 billion are tiny. 

But boosting Chinese FDI will require tolerance of some minimal level of insecurity on Europe’s part. Otherwise, the pursuit of absolute security will come at an economic price that is just too high, and will, in the end, be self-defeating. FDI may well be the best way to build on the economic peace that is trying to break out.

item.title: Even if US democracy can be salvaged from Trump, Europe is moving on | Rafael Behr
item.description:
It will take decades to rebuild trust in a country that removed a tyrant once – and then reinstated him four years later

When Joe Biden entered the White House in 2021 it was possible to believe that Donald Trump’s reign had been an aberration. “America is back. The transatlantic alliance is back,” the new president declared to relieved European leaders shortly after winning the 2020 race. It was true, but not for long.

Trump’s defeat proved that US democracy was mechanically operational, not culturally robust. His supporters tried violent subversion to prevent the inauguration of a successor. A second term should have been unthinkable. Republicans who failed to denounce the 6 January insurrection should have been unelectable. Instead, within four years, US voters reinstated the champion of a failed coup against their cherished constitution as commander-in-chief.

Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist
